NOTES.text:
Core explanation · 00:00–04:59

Today we are going to learn about unit one.

Key details

  • In that, topic one, an introduction to semiconductor.
  • The three semiconductors which is most commonly or most frequently used in the construction of electronic devices are germanium, silicon, and gallium arsenide.
  • And we also see that the atomic structure of silicon and germanium.
  • First, if you look at the atomic structure of silicon, the atomic number is 14, and it's represented in terms of SPDF model one S two, two S two, two P six, three S two.
  • And if you start arranging with respect to the shell around, we call it as orbits.
  • So the first orbit can have two, second can have eight, and the remaining four, that is three S two, three P two are at the outside.
  • We call it as a valence shell, which has four valence electron.
  • That means to say, they are not stable.
  • But before that, they try to balance by themselves by moving from lower energy level to the higher energy level.
  • There is a no gap at all.
  • There's an overlapping in the case of a conductor between the conduction band and the valence band.
  • Whereas in the case of a semiconductor, as we see, there is a little gap compared to the insulator and conductor.
  • The term intrinsic is applied to any semiconductor material that carefully refine to reduce the number of impurities to a very low level.
  • That is, we can call it as a pure form, made available through modern technology.
  • Whereas extrinsic semiconductor are those that can be subjected to doping process with the impurities being added to that.
  • Even in the upper part, even in the lower, even in the lower and also the side we see that there is a covalent bond where valence electrons are shared.
  • With the increase in the voltage, the semiconductor act like a conductor where covalent bond is ruptured, with the temperature reduced act like an insulator where the covalent bonds are not ruptured.
  • We know the four valence electrons are shared with the neighboring silicon atom, and one is free, the fifth valence electron of the antimony is free.
  • And if you apply the voltage to this bonding arrangement, and covalent bond is ruptured, one more electrons will get free up.
  • That means the number of electrons are more compared to the holes here.

Example or application from the lecture

  • Similarly, any semiconductor material, if you look at example again, germanium 32, the outermost valence electron will be four again.
  • For example, if you look at the first diagram here, as marked here, where the impurity added is the antimony impurity has been added, where outermost five valence electrons are there.

Core explanation · 05:00–09:59

No covalent bond is formed, so already there exists one bond.

Key details

  • With the addition of an impurity over there, results in one hole.
  • With the further change, means you say with applied voltage, one more covalent bond is ruptured, and a free electron is released and a hole is introduced over there.
  • The positive charge material is formed with the introduction of a trivalent impurity with the three valence electron such as boron, gallium, and indium materials.
  • We can construct our first solid state electronic device, that is a semiconductor diode, by sandwiching P-type and N-type material together to form a depletion region between the two.
  • It is a fabrication of one material with majority charge carrier of electron to one with majority carrier of holes.
  • How do we do a biasing of a diode?
  • Where we go for forward bias and reverse bias.
  • In a forward bias, a material type connected to the same polarity terminal of a voltage source.
  • Whereas the reverse bias, a material type connected to a opposite polarity terminal of the voltage source.
  • As shown in the diagram now, a P-type and N-type material sandwich with the depletion region form.
  • P terminal and a N region is connected to the negative terminal, then it's said to be the forward bias.
  • And if you reverse this, it's called as a reverse bias.
  • We see the different type of diodes in the diagram here.
  • Various companies have come up with the various structures of diodes here as we see.
  • It could be a two terminal or a three terminal also sometime.
  • IC-based diodes, which could be designed by the different companies.

Example or application from the lecture

  • Next, let us see what is a diode, where diode is one which has a two airports.
